## Summary

Roll-up for initiative INIT-2026-11-18-ppa-v1: extract all formal and practical intelligence from Principles of Program Analysis into a vendor-neutral L0–L3 knowledge package with lossless issue tracking, deterministic validators, harness adapters and 11 adversarial gates. Child shards: ISS-W0-01, ISS-W0-02, ISS-W0-03, ISS-W1-01, ISS-W1-02, ISS-W2-01, ISS-W2-02, ISS-W2-03, ISS-W2-04, ISS-W3-01, ISS-W3-02, ISS-W4-01, ISS-W4-02, ISS-W5-01, ISS-W5-02, ISS-W5-03, ISS-W6-01, ISS-W6-02, ISS-W7-01, ISS-W8-01, ISS-W8-02.

## Source Citations & Grounding

- Whole book (book pp. 1–452; PDF pp. 21–465; 465 PDF pages)
- Coordinate source of truth: `corpus/pdf_page_map.json` (variable PDF offset; never assume a constant offset).

## Technical Analysis / Mechanism

Target altitudes: L0, L1, L2, L3. Altitudes per architecture/ARCHITECTURE.md §3.1: R0 always-on = 0 bytes; L0 = zero always-on bytes (router 50–99L and ambient 80–250L files loaded on match only); L1 = references (<=450L) with every side condition preserved; L2 = actionable skill procedures (250–499L) with explicit precondition checks; L3 = corpus shards and concept graph.

## Acceptance Gates

- [ ] Artifact `MASTER_PLAN.md` exists and passes `scripts/validate_ppa_knowledge.py`

- [ ] `python3 -B scripts/check_portability_hygiene.py .` exits 0

_Pending._

- Parent: none; depends on: none; blocks: none
- `MASTER_PLAN.md`
- `issues/shards/`

## Summary

Adding S → S leaves the inductive reading of Example B.2 unchanged but makes the coinductive reading all of {0,1,2}^∞; lfp and gfp coincide for the contractive functional 𝒬₀ but not for 𝒬₁–𝒬₃. Excluding strings containing 2 from the coinductive reading uses an inductive argument.

## Source Citations & Grounding

- [PPA Example B.2, p. 415] (book p. 415; PDF p. 431)
- [PPA §B.2, p. 410] (book p. 410; PDF p. 426)
- [PPA Example B.2, p. 414] (book p. 414; PDF p. 430)
- Statements confirmed against rendered page images during Unit 0 extraction.

## Technical Analysis / Mechanism

Checkers that accept a goal already on the visited stack implement gfp; an unguarded self-reference (A trusts A, type T = T) is then accepted, widening acceptance to everything (G-U0-25). By §B.2 (p. 410), requiring recursive calls to strictly decrease along a well-founded order (such as (ℕ, <) for 𝒬₀) collapses lfp = gfp (G-U0-21) — whereas on non-well-founded infinite strings {0,1,2}^∞ (Example B.2), productive constructor-guarded rules admit {0,1}^ω under gfp without collapsing to lfp. Conversely, assuming gfp-defined sets need only coinductive reasoning misses the inductive step of Example B.2.

Guardrail: L2: state whether a recursive specification uses lfp or gfp; reject unguarded trivial self-rules in coinductive checkers by requiring productive/constructor-guarded recursion `[external]` (whereas strictly decreasing recursion along a well-founded order forces lfp = gfp).

## Summary

Table C.1 and the dominator definition assume a handle H from which every node is reachable; Example C.6 states that final(S) is a handle of the backward flow graph `(labels(S), flowᴿ(S))` for WHILE statements (which holds unconditionally by structural syntax because `final(while [b]^ℓ do S₀) = {ℓ}`).

## Source Citations & Grounding

- [PPA §C.1, p. 419] (book p. 419; PDF p. 434)
- [PPA §C.1, p. 420] (book p. 420; PDF p. 435)
- [PPA Table C.1, p. 421] (book p. 421; PDF p. 436)
- Statements confirmed against rendered page images during Unit 0 extraction (G-U0-30, G-U0-31).

## Technical Analysis / Mechanism

In WHILE, `flow(S)` and `final(S)` are purely syntactic, so even semantically non-terminating loops (`while [true]^1 do [skip]^2`) remain syntactically reachable from `final(S)` in `flowᴿ(S)`. By contrast, in general compiler/binary CFGs `[external]`, dead blocks or undiscovered indirect-jump targets are unreachable from the entry (so DFS leaves them unnumbered and greatest-solution dominator equations give them `Dom(n) = N`), and syntactic exit-less sink loops (e.g. `for(;;)` with no `break`/`return` edge) leave loop nodes unreachable from exit blocks in the backward CFG, invalidating naive post-dominance claims (`[external]`).

Guardrail: L2: verify the handle covers every node (add a dummy root for multiple entries); track unreachable components explicitly instead of letting them inherit ⊤.

## Summary

Back edges and d(G, T) are defined relative to a DFSF T; Lemma C.12 makes them coincide with dominator-back edges only for reducible graphs; Example C.13 equates d(G) with the maximum loop nesting depth for uniquely labelled WHILE statements.

## Source Citations & Grounding

- [PPA §C.2, p. 424] (book p. 424; PDF p. 439)
- [PPA Figure C.3, p. 425] (book p. 425; PDF p. 440)

For Figure C.3, which of the two edges between n₁ and n₂ is a back edge depends on T (though symmetric Figure C.3 happens to have d(G, T) = 1 under both DFSFs, larger irreducible multi-entry graphs have T-dependent d(G, T)). Without unique labels on WHILE blocks, distinct blocks collapse into one node and can break reducibility and the nesting-depth identity. Sibling loops do not add up (Figure C.1 has two loops and d(G) = 1).

Guardrail: L1/L2: always write d(G, T) with its forest, distinguish 'back edge' from 'dominator-back edge', and restrict the nesting-depth reading to reducible graphs (see BKL-010).

## Summary

Back edges and d(G, T) are defined relative to a DFSF T; Lemma C.12 makes them coincide with dominator-back edges only for reducible graphs; Example C.13 equates d(G) with the maximum loop nesting depth for uniquely labelled WHILE statements.

## Source Citations & Grounding

- [PPA §C.2, p. 424] (book p. 424; PDF p. 439)
- [PPA Figure C.3, p. 425] (book p. 425; PDF p. 440)
- [PPA Lemma C.12, p. 425] (book p. 425; PDF p. 440)
- [PPA Example C.13, p. 425] (book p. 425; PDF p. 440)
- Statements confirmed against rendered page images during Unit 0 extraction (G-U0-40, G-U0-41, G-U0-42).

## Technical Analysis / Mechanism

For Figure C.3, which of the two edges between n₁ and n₂ is a back edge depends on T (though symmetric Figure C.3 happens to have d(G, T) = 1 under both DFSFs, larger irreducible multi-entry graphs have T-dependent d(G, T)). Without unique labels on WHILE blocks, distinct blocks collapse into one node and can break reducibility and the nesting-depth identity. Sibling loops do not add up (Figure C.1 has two loops and d(G) = 1).

Guardrail: L1/L2: always write d(G, T) with its forest, distinguish 'back edge' from 'dominator-back edge', and restrict the nesting-depth reading to reducible graphs (see BKL-010).

## Summary

BExp grammar includes true and false and §2.1 uses [true]^{ℓ'}, yet Table 2.5 omits ℬ⟦true⟧σ = true and ℬ⟦false⟧σ = false.

## Source Citations & Grounding

Table 2.5 defines boolean valuation `ℬ⟦b⟧σ` across negation (`not`), conjunction (`and`/`or`), and relational comparisons `a₁ op_r a₂`, while omitting the base literal equations `ℬ⟦true⟧σ = true` and `ℬ⟦false⟧σ = false` despite `true`/`false` appearing in the `BExp` syntax (`Table 1.2` / `§2.1`) and in `[true]^{ℓ'}` loop examples (`§2.1.2`). ## Summary

LV^⊆ on p. 60 suppresses flow^R edges at final(S⋆) without stating isolated exits, causing trailing while-loops and [seq₁]/[seq₂] sub-statements to violate Lemma 2.18 and Theorem 2.21.

## Source Citations & Grounding

- [PPA §2.2.2, p. 60] (book p. 60; PDF p. 79)
- [PPA Lemma 2.18, p. 61] (book p. 61; PDF p. 80)
- [PPA Theorem 2.21, p. 64] (book p. 64; PDF p. 83)
- Statements confirmed against rendered page images during Unit 2 extraction.

## Technical Analysis / Mechanism

Because `p. 60` defines `LV_exit(ℓ) ⊇ ∅` whenever `ℓ ∈ final(S⋆)` (using `⋃{LV_entry(ℓ') | (ℓ', ℓ) ∈ flow^R(S⋆)}` only `otherwise`), any program ending in a loop—such as `S = while [x>0]^1 do [x:=x-y]^2` where `final(S) = {1}` and `(1, 2) ∈ flow(S)`—gives `live_exit(1) = ∅ ⊉ {x, y} = live_entry(2)`. This yields a concrete counterexample to `Lemma 2.18` and breaks `Theorem 2.21(i)` under step `[wh₁]` (`σ₁ = {x↦1, y↦0}` and `σ₂ = {x↦1, y↦5}` satisfy `σ₁ ∼_{N(1)} σ₂`, then diverge on `N(2) = {x, y}`), as well as `[seq₁]`/`[seq₂]` sub-statements whose internal `while` bodies lack isolated exits even when the outer `S⋆` has isolated exits.

Guardrail: Always formulate constraints unconditionally as LV_exit(ℓ) ⊇ ⋃{...} ⊔ ι^ℓ_E (§2.3) in both solvers and proofs. (Refs: F-U2a-09, G-U2a-18, G-U2a-19).

## Summary

Example 2.30 states h <= v*b overlooking the v initial pairs (x, ?) (so h <= v*(b+1)), and label consistency gives h <= b+v -> O(b^2) when v = O(b).

## Source Citations & Grounding

- [PPA Example 2.30, p. 78] (book p. 78; PDF p. 97)
- Statements confirmed against rendered page images during Unit 2 extraction.

## Technical Analysis / Mechanism

Each variable `x ∈ Var⋆` can carry its uninitialised reaching pair `(x, ?)` alongside labelled definitions `(x, ℓ)` (`|Lab⋆^?| = b + 1`), so the full height of `(𝒫(Var⋆ × Lab⋆^?), ⊆)` is `h ≤ v · (b + 1)` rather than `v · b`. Even under label consistency (where each label `ℓ` maps to at most one assigned variable `x`, giving `b` labelled pairs), there remain up to `v` distinct uninitialised pairs `(x, ?)`, yielding `h ≤ b + v` and total worklist complexity `O(e · (b + v)) = O(b · (b + v))`; `O(b²)` holds only under the hidden regularity assumption `v = O(b)`.

Guardrail: Include (x, ?) in lattice height accounting and state v = O(b) side condition when quoting O(b^2). (Refs: F-U2a-14, G-U2a-31).

## Summary

Example 2.30 states h <= v*b overlooking the v initial pairs (x, ?) (so h <= v*(b+1)), and label consistency gives h <= b+v -> O(b^2) when v = O(b).

## Source Citations & Grounding

- [PPA Example 2.30, p. 78] (book p. 78; PDF p. 97)
- Statements confirmed against rendered page images during Unit 2 extraction.

## Technical Analysis / Mechanism

Each variable `x ∈ Var⋆` can carry its uninitialised reaching pair `(x, ?)` alongside labelled definitions `(x, ℓ)` (`|Lab⋆^?| = b + 1`), so the full height of `(𝒫(Var⋆ × Lab⋆^?), ⊆)` is `h ≤ v · (b + 1)` rather than `v · b`. Even under label consistency (where each label `ℓ` maps to at most one assigned variable `x`, giving `b` labelled pairs), there remain up to `v` distinct uninitialised pairs `(x, ?)`, yielding `h ≤ b + v` and total worklist complexity `O(e · (b + v)) = O(b · (b + v))`; `O(b²)` holds only under the hidden regularity assumption `v = O(b)`.

issues.body:
## Summary

§2.5 embellishes a monotone framework, yet the book itself flags an important snag: the call and return transfer functions for large assumption sets are in general not monotone.

## Source Citations & Grounding

- [PPA §2.5, p. 100] (book p. 100; PDF p. 119)
- [PPA Lemma 2.29, p. 75] (book p. 75; PDF p. 94)
- [PPA §2.4, p. 76] (book p. 76; PDF p. 95)
- [PPA §2.4, p. 77] (book p. 77; PDF p. 96)
- [PPA Chapter 2 Concluding Remarks, p. 129] (book p. 129; PDF p. 148)
- Coordinates validated against `corpus/pdf_page_map.json`; formulas must be confirmed against the rendered page image (see BKL-011).

## Technical Analysis / Mechanism

Adding a fact at a call site replaces the exact context key instead of extending it, so f(Z1) ⊑ f(Z2) can fail for Z1 ⊑ Z2 (derived from the definitions on p. 100). Termination of the worklist algorithm is not lost: the termination part of the proof of Lemma 2.29 uses only that each update joins into a strictly larger value and that the lattice satisfies the Ascending Chain Condition [PPA Lemma 2.29, p. 75] (book p. 75; PDF p. 94), [PPA §2.4, p. 76] (book p. 76; PDF p. 95). What is lost is the guarantee that the result is the least (MFP) solution: the correctness part of the proof uses the monotonicity of the transfer functions [PPA §2.4, p. 77] (book p. 77; PDF p. 96).

Guardrail: L2: treat the snag as a precision and least-solution issue, not a non-termination issue, and pick one of the book's remedies: (1) solving techniques for weakly monotonic systems of equations, referenced in the Concluding Remarks [PPA Chapter 2 Concluding Remarks, p. 129] (book p. 129; PDF p. 148); (2) the more approximate, monotone definition that relaxes the equality on the context component to an inclusion; (3) small assumption sets [PPA §2.5, p. 100] (book p. 100; PDF p. 119). Never feed exact large-assumption-set context keys into a monotone solver without stating the snag.

## Summary

§2.5 instantiates backward interprocedural analysis with F = flow⋆^R, E = final⋆, IF = inter-flow⋆^R without defining ^R on semicolon flows or 4-tuples.

## Source Citations & Grounding

- [PPA §2.5, p. 85] (book p. 85; PDF p. 104)
- Statements confirmed against rendered page images during Unit 2 extraction.

## Technical Analysis / Mechanism

Forward `§2.5` distinguishes semicolon interprocedural call/return arcs `(ℓ_c; ℓ_n)` and `(ℓ_x; ℓ_r)` in `flow⋆` from matched 4-tuples `(ℓ_c, ℓ_n, ℓ_x, ℓ_r)` in `inter-flow⋆`. Page 85 notes briefly that backward analyses take `F = flow⋆^R`, `E = final⋆`, and `IF = inter-flow⋆^R` without spelling out the reversal rules: orienting semicolon arcs backwards gives `(ℓ_n; ℓ_c)` and `(ℓ_r; ℓ_x)`, while reversing 4-tuples flips both control endpoints and entry/exit roles to `(ℓ_r, ℓ_x, ℓ_n, ℓ_c)` so post-call liveness propagates backward through callee exit `ℓ_x` to call entry `ℓ_c` while restoring pre-return caller facts via `f̂²`.

## Summary

Rewritten [ass] and bind's trailing z:=y omit elementary-block labels, and [call] implies distinct ξ₁ ≠ ξ₂ for val/res formals without explicitly writing ξ₁ ≠ ξ₂.

## Source Citations & Grounding

- [PPA §2.5.1, p. 86] (book p. 86; PDF p. 105)
- [PPA §2.5.1, p. 87] (book p. 87; PDF p. 106)
- Statements confirmed against rendered page images during Unit 2 extraction.

## Technical Analysis / Mechanism

Two-level SOS (`§2.5.1`) evaluates `[call p(a, z)]^{ℓ_c}_{ℓ_r}` into intermediate term `bind ρ⋆[x ↦ ξ₁, y ↦ ξ₂] in S then z := y`. Neither the trailing copy `z := y` nor the rewritten `[ass]` assignment carries a syntactic `Lab` label—breaking naive invariant proofs that assume every intermediate step has an entry/exit label (deferred by the authors to Chapter 3 closure semantics). ## Summary

With L=𝒫(D), ι ⊆ D so printed ι̂ = {({ι}, ι)} and {(ι, ι)} are ill-typed unless ι is identified with a single d₀; Example 2.41 drops braces and formals u, v and varies y instead of u.

## Source Citations & Grounding

- [PPA §2.5.5, p. 99] (book p. 99; PDF p. 118)
- [PPA Example 2.41, p. 99] (book p. 99; PDF p. 118)
- [PPA §2.5.5, p. 100] (book p. 100; PDF p. 119)
- Statements confirmed against rendered page images during Unit 2 extraction.

## Technical Analysis / Mechanism

For `L = 𝒫(D)` in `§2.5.5`, the extremal element `ι` is already a subset `ι ⊆ D`. Writing `ι̂ = {({ι}, ι)}` (Large) and `{(ι, ι)}` (Small) commits a set-level type mismatch whenever `|ι| ≠ 1`, because `Δ = 𝒫(D)` expects `(δ ∈ 𝒫(D), d ∈ D)` pairs and `Δ = D` expects `(d₁ ∈ D, d₂ ∈ D)` pairs. Additionally, `Example 2.41` writes 3-component state tuples (`(u, a, ...)` without formal parameters `(x, y)` on Fibonacci's 5-variable store) and varies `y` instead of `u`, obscuring the non-monotonicity witness (`Z₁ = {(δ₀, d₁)} ⊆ Z₂ = {(δ₀, d₁), (δ₀, d₂)}` shrinks `{d'' | (δ, d'') ∈ Z}` output tags).

Guardrail: Use well-typed {(ι, d) | d ∈ ι} (large) and {(d, d) | d ∈ ι} (small), plus monotone ⊆ or small assumption sets (BKL-003). (Refs: F-U2b-06, G-U2b-12, G-U2b-13, BKL-003).

## Summary

Boolean guards [not is-nil(x)] act as identity, Case 1 maps nil-deref in [x:=y.sel] to {kill_x(...)} without raising a fault, and absent GC inflates 𝒫(SG) past 50 graphs on 7-block list reversal.

## Source Citations & Grounding

- [PPA §2.6.3, p. 116] (book p. 116; PDF p. 135)
- [PPA §2.6.3, p. 120] (book p. 120; PDF p. 139)
- [PPA Exercise 2.21, p. 139] (book p. 139; PDF p. 158)
- Statements confirmed against rendered page images during Unit 2 extraction.

## Technical Analysis / Mechanism

Three operational pitfalls limit naive `§2.6` implementations: (1) Boolean tests such as `[not is-nil(x)]` act as identity transfers, failing to prune null branches; (2) `[x := y.sel]` Case 1 silently maps null/missing-selector dereferences to `{kill_x(...)}` rather than aborting or emitting a fault, allowing post-crash paths to survive; (3) Neither `kill_x` nor `kill_{x.sel}` removes unreachable nodes from `n_∅`, pushing simple 7-block list reversal (`Exercise* 2.21`) above 50 abstract shape graphs unless GC, allocation-site naming (`n_{ℓ,X}`), or single-summary merging is introduced.

Guardrail: Emit client null-deref diagnostics from Shape∘(ℓ) before Case 1 transfer, pair with [b]^{ℓ₁,ℓ₂} branch splits, and adopt GC / n_{ℓ,X} / single-summary merging [148, 149]. (Refs: G-U2b-17, G-U2b-23, G-U2b-24, G-U2b-28).

## Summary

Uniform k-CFA has exponential worst-case complexity for positive k; the book separately discusses a polynomial variant and the Cartesian Product Algorithm.

## Source Citations & Grounding

- [PPA Table 3.10, p. 192] (book p. 192; PDF p. 210)
- [PPA §3.6, p. 195] (book p. 195; PDF p. 213)
- [PPA §3.6, p. 196] (book p. 196; PDF p. 214)
- Coordinates validated against `corpus/pdf_page_map.json`; formulas must be confirmed against the rendered page image (see BKL-011).

## Technical Analysis / Mechanism

The book relates the interprocedural analysis of §2.5 (call strings) and uniform k-CFA: their abstract caches "have the same overall functionality" and "the two analyses are variations over a theme" [PPA §3.6, p. 196] (book p. 196; PDF p. 214). The book does not compare their costs. [external] In practice the cost of call-string context differs between first-order data flow and higher-order control flow analysis; summaries that present k-CFA as a cheap refinement smooth away the exponential worst-case bound the book states for uniform k-CFA with k > 0.

## Summary

The book evaluates arithmetic over unbounded integers and states that no errors can occur (division by 0 must still produce an integer); the Interval lattice ranges over integers extended with infinities. [external] Machine arithmetic wraps modulo 2^w or is undefined on signed overflow; the book does not discuss machine arithmetic.

## Source Citations & Grounding

- [PPA Table 2.5, p. 55] (book p. 55; PDF p. 74)
- [PPA §4.2, p. 221] (book p. 221; PDF p. 238)
- Coordinates validated against `corpus/pdf_page_map.json`; formulas must be confirmed against the rendered page image (see BKL-011).

## Technical Analysis / Mechanism

[external] An Interval transfer function sound over the integers is unsound over 32/64-bit two's-complement values: [0, MAX] + [1, 1] is [1, MAX+1] mathematically but wraps negative at runtime, defeating upper-bound checks; folding that relies on signed-overflow UB can delete overflow guards.

Guardrail: L2 procedures that reuse Interval/Sign analyses on machine integers must state the wrap-around model (wrapped intervals [external]) or add explicit overflow proof obligations; division by zero is a fault sink.

## Summary

Upper bound operators (and hence widenings) are explicitly not required to be monotone, commutative, associative or absorptive.

## Source Citations & Grounding

- [PPA §4.2, p. 225] (book p. 225; PDF p. 242)
- [PPA §4.2, p. 226] (book p. 226; PDF p. 243)
- [PPA Chapter 6 Exercises, p. 391] (book p. 391; PDF p. 407)
- Coordinates validated against `corpus/pdf_page_map.json`; formulas must be confirmed against the rendered page image (see BKL-011).

## Technical Analysis / Mechanism

A widening operator is an upper bound operator [PPA §4.2, p. 226] (book p. 226; PDF p. 243), and upper bound operators are not required to be monotone [PPA §4.2, p. 225] (book p. 225; PDF p. 242). A summary that treats widening as monotone therefore states a property the book does not give: a larger input to ∇ need not give a larger result, and ∇ need not be commutative (the book's interval example on p. 225 gives different results for swapped arguments), so precision of the widened iteration can depend on the order in which values arrive. Exercise 6.13 asks for a worklist algorithm with widening and for proofs that it over-approximates the least solution and terminates even without the Ascending Chain Condition. Note that x ⊔ (x ∇ y) = x ∇ y, because x ∇ y ⊒ x for an upper bound operator; that wrapping is not a hazard.

Guardrail: L2: never claim that a widening operator is monotone, commutative, associative or absorptive; quote the termination argument for the widened iteration, not a monotonicity argument. [external] In chaotic-iteration solvers, apply widening only at cycle cut points (e.g. targets of back edges for a depth-first spanning forest) and follow with narrowing where precision matters.

## Summary

Exception analysis subtracts handled exceptions from effects (rule [handle], Table 5.10). On an effect variable the book defines β\{s} = β, even though β might later be instantiated to {s} [PPA §5.4, p. 329] (book p. 329; PDF p. 346). Generalisation must not quantify variables free in the effect (illustrated by Example 5.36).

## Source Citations & Grounding

- [PPA Table 5.10, p. 328] (book p. 328; PDF p. 345)
- [PPA §5.4, p. 329] (book p. 329; PDF p. 346)
- [PPA §5.4, p. 330] (book p. 330; PDF p. 347)
- [PPA Example 5.36, p. 346] (book p. 346; PDF p. 363)
- Coordinates validated against `corpus/pdf_page_map.json`; formulas must be confirmed against the rendered page image (see BKL-011).

## Technical Analysis / Mechanism

Per the book, β\{s} = β is semantically sound, because β\{s} ⊆ β should hold for all instantiations of β (as in rule [sub]); "to define a less approximate system" it would be natural to add φ ::= ··· | φ\{s} and extend the UCAI axiomatisation to set difference [PPA §5.4, p. 330] (book p. 330; PDF p. 347). Erasing the subtraction on effect variables is therefore sound but less precise; keeping φ\{s} symbolically is the more precise option. [external] Dropping the generalisation side condition admits type confusion through polymorphic channels and references.

Guardrail: L2: enforce the generalisation side condition explicitly; accept β\{s} = β as the sound default, and where precision matters represent subtraction on effect variables symbolically (φ\{s}) with the extended axiomatisation.

## Summary

Uniquely labelled WHILE programs yield reducible graphs (Example C.13); Figure C.3 shows an irreducible graph. For instances of a Bit Vector Framework iterated in reverse postorder of a depth-first spanning forest T, the Round Robin bound of Lemma 6.12 (`d(G_S, T) + 3` iterations) is stated in terms of the loop connectedness parameter `d(G_S, T)`.

## Source Citations & Grounding

- [PPA Lemma 6.12, p. 380] (book p. 380; PDF p. 396)
- [PPA Figure C.3, p. 425] (book p. 425; PDF p. 440)
- [PPA Lemma C.12, p. 425] (book p. 425; PDF p. 440)
- [PPA Example C.13, p. 425] (book p. 425; PDF p. 440)
- Coordinates validated against `corpus/pdf_page_map.json`; formulas must be confirmed against the rendered page image (see BKL-011).

## Technical Analysis / Mechanism

[external] Binaries, goto-heavy C and obfuscated code produce irreducible graphs in which back edges depend on the spanning forest, natural-loop headers are ill-defined, and `d(G_S, T)` varies with the chosen DFSF `T`; moreover, non-bit-vector frameworks do not inherit Lemma 6.12's `d(G_S, T) + 3` cap.

Guardrail: L2: use strong components (§6.3) rather than structural reduction; quote `d(G_S, T) + 3` only for Bit Vector Framework instances with DFSF `T` and reverse postorder; [external] place widening at DFSF back-edge targets.
